objectives: Trace wine's origins from the Caucasus through antiquity and medieval monasticism to the modern era.
Explain the etymology and evolution of the sommelier role and the major credentialing bodies.
Describe the Judgment of Paris 1976 and why deductive blind tasting is the cornerstone of professional evaluation.

slides.title: Eight thousand years in a glass — wine from the Caucasus to the courts of Europe
slides.body:
Wine is among the oldest biotechnologies humans ever discovered. The earliest archaeochemical evidence comes from **Georgia** in the South Caucasus: analysis of pottery sherds from the Neolithic site of **Gadachrili Gora** (published 2017 in *PNAS* by Patrick McGovern's team at the University of Pennsylvania Museum) dates tartaric acid residues — the chemical fingerprint of *Vitis vinifera* — to approximately **6000 BC**. Clay **qvevri** (large egg-shaped earthenware vessels still used in Georgian natural wine production today) were buried in the earth and sealed with beeswax, exploiting ambient temperature to control fermentation and aging. Georgia's claim is now widely accepted as the earliest confirmed wine-making culture.

Independent evidence surfaces across the ancient Near East: **Hajji Firuz Tepe** in northwestern Iran (McGovern et al., 1996, *Nature*) yielded wine residues dated to **5400–5000 BC**. **Mesopotamian** cylinder seals and texts reference wine in royal tribute lists; **Egypt** elevated wine to a sacred substance — hieroglyphic records at **Abydos** document royal vineyards circa **3000 BC**, and amphorae from **Tutankhamun's tomb** (c. 1323 BC) bore labels specifying vineyard, vintage, and winemaker — the world's first known wine labels.

**Greek and Roman wine culture** systematised viticulture across the Mediterranean. The Greeks worshipped **Dionysus**, god of wine and ecstasy; the Romans adapted him as **Bacchus**. Roman agronomists — notably **Columella** (*De Re Rustica*, c. AD 65) and **Pliny the Elder** (*Naturalis Historia*, AD 77) — documented grape varieties, pruning methods, and regional quality hierarchies with a sophistication that prefigures modern appellation thinking. Roman **amphorae** (sealed clay transport vessels stamped with origin, vintage, and producer) were the ancient world's appellation system; wrecks on the Mediterranean seafloor have been carbon-dated and their amphora stamps cross-referenced to reconstruct ancient trade routes.

**Medieval monastic viticulture** preserved and systematised wine after Rome's fall. The **Benedictines** (founded at Monte Cassino, AD 529 by **St Benedict of Nursia**) operated vineyards across Europe as a matter of liturgical necessity — wine was required for the Eucharist. The **Cistercians**, a reform order founded at **Cîteaux** in Burgundy in **1098**, took monastic terroir observation to its logical extreme. Working the soils of the **Côte d'Or** by hand over centuries, Cistercian monks at **Clos de Vougeot** (walled vineyard, *clos*, established 1336) identified soil and microclimate differences so precisely that they effectively mapped what became Burgundy's **premier cru** and **grand cru** hierarchy — the concept of a **climat** (a named, bounded parcel with distinct character) was their intellectual invention. The Cistercian abbey at **Kloster Eberbach** in the **Rheingau** played the same role for German Riesling cultivation.

slides.title: The sommelier — from beast of burden to Master of Wine
slides.body:
The word **sommelier** derives from the Old French *somme*, meaning a pack load or burden, itself from the Latin *sagma* (a packsaddle), via the Late Latin *bête de somme* — a beast of burden. The *sommelier* was originally a court official responsible for **provisioning**: overseeing the transport and storage of supplies, including the royal wine cellar. By the 14th century French royal household records distinguish the *sommelier de corps* (personal attendant) from the *sommelier du vin* (wine steward). The role evolved through the aristocratic household economy into the professional restaurant sommelier of the 19th-century Parisian dining scene — a professional who selected, cellared, and presented wine to guests, wielding the *tastevin* (a shallow silver cup used to assess clarity by candlelight before electric cellar lighting existed).

Professional credentialing arrived in the 20th century via three major institutions:

- **Institute of Masters of Wine (IMW)**: founded in London in **1953** by the British wine trade. The **Master of Wine (MW)** qualification remains the most academically demanding in the wine world — candidates must pass written theory papers, a blind tasting examination, and submit an original **research paper** of publishable quality. As of 2024 there are approximately 420 MWs worldwide. Notable MWs include **Jancis Robinson MW**, author of *The Oxford Companion to Wine* (1994; 4th ed. 2015), and **Hugh Johnson MW**, co-author of *The World Atlas of Wine* (1971; 8th ed. 2019).

- **Wine & Spirit Education Trust (WSET)**: established in London in **1969**. WSET offers a four-level qualification ladder (Levels 1-4, with Level 4 Diploma being the entry point to MW study) and educates over **100,000 students per year** in more than 70 countries. The **Systematic Approach to Tasting (SAT)** — a structured protocol covering appearance, nose, and palate — is the WSET's core analytical framework.

- **Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS)**: founded in the UK in **1977**, with the first Master Sommelier exam held that year. The CMS focuses specifically on **restaurant service** — candidates are assessed on theory, blind tasting, and practical service (decanting, wine and food pairing, hospitality). The **Master Sommelier (MS)** diploma is the apex; as of 2024 fewer than 280 individuals hold it globally. The American chapter (established 1987) became the dominant certification body for US restaurant sommeliers; the documentary *SOMM* (2012, dir. Jason Wise) brought the MS exam to public attention.

The **tastevin**, the **decanter**, and the **sommelier's knife** (waiter's friend corkscrew) remain the symbolic tools of the trade, though the profession now encompasses cellar management, wine list design, producer relationships, and **deductive blind tasting** — the analytical method by which a trained palate identifies grape variety, region, vintage, and producer from sensory data alone.

slides.title: The Judgment of Paris 1976 and the logic of deductive tasting
slides.body:
On **24 May 1976** a British wine merchant named **Steven Spurrier** — then operating the Académie du Vin wine school in Paris — organised a blind tasting in which nine eminent French judges compared **California wines against top French wines** in two flights: red (Cabernet Sauvignon-based) and white (Chardonnay). The judges believed they were tasting blind but assumed French wines would win; they were wrong on every count.

In the **red flight**, the **1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars S.L.V. Cabernet Sauvignon** (Napa Valley, winemaker **Warren Winiarski**) took first place over the **1970 Château Mouton Rothschild** and **1970 Château Montrose**. In the **white flight**, the **1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay** (Napa Valley, winemaker **Miljenko 'Mike' Grgich**) beat the **1973 Meursault Charmes** (Domaine Roulot) and the **1972 Bâtard-Montrachet** (Ramonet-Prudhon). The only journalist present was **George Taber** of *Time* magazine, whose subsequent article (June 7, 1976, 'Judgment of Paris') broke the story to the world. The event is widely credited with establishing California — and by extension the New World — as capable of producing wines of the highest quality, triggering massive investment in Napa Valley and restructuring the global fine wine market.

**Deductive blind tasting** is the analytical discipline that underlies both professional credentialing and the Judgment of Paris. The deductive method proceeds from sensory observations to reasoned conclusions:

1. **Appearance**: colour depth and hue (indicates grape, age, climate); clarity; viscosity (legs/tears indicate alcohol and glycerol content).
2. **Nose**: primary aromas (fruit, floral, herb — from the grape itself); secondary aromas (yeast-derived: brioche, cream, biscuit); tertiary aromas / bouquet (oak, oxidation, bottle age: vanilla, cedar, leather, petrol, earthiness).
3. **Palate**: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavour intensity, flavour characteristics, finish (length in seconds).
4. **Conclusions**: grape variety (single or blend?), origin (Old World or New World? specific region?), vintage (young or aged?), quality level, readiness to drink.

The **WSET SAT** and the **CMS deductive tasting grid** formalise this sequence. The best sommeliers combine sensory memory built over thousands of tasted wines with probabilistic reasoning: "high acidity + green apple + no oak + bone dry = likely Chablis or Muscadet, probably not New World Chardonnay." **Jancis Robinson** describes the process as "thinking aloud with your nose."

The Judgment of Paris was itself a lesson in the limits of expectation bias — the French judges marked down wines they couldn't identify as French, revealing that even expert palates are susceptible to **confirmation bias**. Blind tasting disciplines out that bias, which is why every major qualification requires it.

question.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the credentialing body with its founding year and primary focus?
options: Court of Master Sommeliers (1953) — academic research papers + blind tasting.
Institute of Masters of Wine (1969) — restaurant service + practical decanting.
Wine & Spirit Education Trust (1969) — tiered education from beginner to diploma, 100 000+ students/year; distinct from the IMW (1953, academic MW) and the CMS (1977, restaurant service).
Court of Master Sommeliers (1977) — academic written papers + original research.
question.explanation: The three pillars of wine education are often confused. The **Institute of Masters of Wine (IMW)** was founded in London in **1953** and awards the **MW** qualification via written theory, blind tasting, and an original research paper — the most academically demanding credential in wine. The **Wine & Spirit Education Trust (WSET)** was established in **1969** and runs a tiered ladder (Levels 1-4 Diploma) educating over 100 000 students per year in 70+ countries; its Level 4 Diploma is the standard entry requirement for MW candidacy. The **Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS)** was founded in **1977** and focuses on **restaurant service** — theory, blind tasting, and practical service (decanting, food pairing, hospitality) — culminating in the **Master Sommelier (MS)** diploma held by fewer than 280 people globally. Knowing these distinctions is essential for any sommelier career path.

hints: Match 1953 to the oldest, most academically demanding credential.
Which body runs the Systematic Approach to Tasting (SAT)?
slides.workedSolution: IMW (1953) = Masters of Wine, research + theory. WSET (1969) = tiered education, SAT framework. CMS (1977) = restaurant service, Master Sommelier diploma. Option C is the only one that correctly pairs WSET with 1969 and accurately describes its scope.

question.question: A guest challenges your blind tasting conclusion
question.prompt: During a CMS-style practical examination, you are presented with a white wine. You conclude it is a 2018 Chablis Premier Cru based on: pale gold colour, high acidity, oyster shell and green apple on the nose, no perceptible oak, bone-dry palate, and moderate alcohol (~12%). The examiner tells you the wine is actually a 2019 Mâcon-Villages (also Chardonnay, also Burgundy). Walk through which sensory cues you got right, which cues led you astray, and how you would recalibrate your deductive tasting framework going forward. Reference the WSET Systematic Approach to Tasting and the role of terroir in shaping Chardonnay's expression across Burgundy appellations.

In ≤150 words, explain why the Cistercian monks at Clos de Vougeot are historically significant to the modern concept of wine terroir, and how that connects to today's sommelier's practice of deductive tasting.
question.rubric: Should articulate: Cistercians mapped soil and microclimate differences in Burgundy over centuries, effectively inventing the concept of the *climat* — a bounded parcel with distinct character — which became the intellectual foundation for appellation systems (AOC, etc.). Should connect this to deductive tasting: a sommelier uses terroir knowledge (soil type, drainage, aspect, mesoclimate) as part of their reasoned conclusion chain — 'Kimmeridgian limestone soils + cool climate + no oak = Chablis.' Bonus: mention Clos de Vougeot (founded 1336), the Cistercian abbey at Cîteaux (1098), or the Côte d'Or as specific references.
